contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Classify unfamiliar stack code from retained-state semantics, a maintained order invariant, the exact removal rule, and its correctness argument—not from names, indices, comparisons, loops, or asymptotic cost alone.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant; human review required

items.prompt: Delimiter validation, Undo history, postfix evaluation, and explicit DFS all use stacks. Which statement explains why this fact alone does not make them monotonic-stack algorithms?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Ordinary nesting, history, evaluation, and traversal all use LIFO without ordered candidates.
Every stack problem is monotonic.
One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.
If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.

feedback.reason: Their entries represent unmatched structures, reversible history, operands, or pending work—not an order-maintained frontier of unresolved candidates.

blocks.text: A delimiter pops on structural closure, Undo pops on a user request, postfix pops by operator arity, and DFS pops pending work. None requires retained values to be monotone or proves a candidate permanently irrelevant through comparison. A temporarily sorted snapshot, linear runtime, or repeated pop loop can occur in these ordinary stacks. Reusable classification rule: require ordered unresolved candidates plus comparison-driven safe removal, not merely LIFO storage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The four counterexamples use LIFO for different semantic triggers and have no required ordered candidate frontier.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Each listed clue also appears in ordinary stacks, so none establishes candidate meaning, invariant, or safe deletion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Incidental order at one instant is not preserved by every legal push and is not connected to any requested answer.

items.prompt: Code names its Undo-history variable `monotonicStack`, but it pushes every committed action and pops only when the user requests Undo. How should the algorithm be classified?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Identifier choice proves algorithm category.
One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.
If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.
Names do not establish maintained order or safe deletion.

feedback.reason: It is an ordinary history stack: actions are retained by recency and no comparison maintains order or proves older actions irrelevant.

blocks.text: Every entry is a committed, not-yet-undone action. A push follows commit order; a pop follows an Undo request. Older actions must remain for later Undo commands, so the algorithm has neither a monotone key nor dominance-based deletion. Renaming the variable cannot change these transitions, and a sorted-looking payload snapshot is incidental. Reusable rule: read entry meaning and pop proof before trusting identifiers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Identifier text has no effect on the history semantics or user-triggered pop rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: No single syntactic clue replaces the missing ordered unresolved frontier.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A later action payload can break any incidental sort while Undo behavior remains correct.

items.prompt: A trace shows retained values in sorted order at one instant. Select all reasons this snapshot is insufficient to prove a monotonic stack.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: A later legal push can break incidental order when no maintenance rule restores it.
Any sorted snapshot is a complete inductive proof of monotonicity.
The variable name determines whether the observed order is meaningful.
An invariant must hold after every legal transition, not only in one observed state.
The order must be tied to unresolved-candidate meaning and the requested output.

feedback.reason: A single sorted state proves neither preservation nor connection between that order, candidate meaning, and the output.

blocks.text: Suppose an operand stack happens to be `[2,5,9]`. A legal next operand `1` produces `[2,5,9,1]` without making evaluation incorrect, proving the order was incidental. A real invariant must hold after every legal transition and explain why retained entries are unresolved candidates and why a comparison pop is safe. Variable naming supplies neither property. All three accepted reasons are therefore necessary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: One state cannot prove preservation; the legal push of `1` is a direct counterexample.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Changing a name does not change transitions or make incidental order semantically relevant.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It distinguishes an invariant from a one-time observation.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It requires order to participate in correctness rather than merely appear.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It supplies a legal future transition that can falsify accidental sortedness.

items.prompt: In asteroid-collision processing, positive values move right and negative values move left. For input `[5,10,-5]`, the top `10` is compared with current `-5`, `-5` is destroyed, and survivors are `[5,10]`. Does the comparison make this a monotonic stack?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.
No. The comparison resolves a local physical collision; survivors are not retained under a global monotone-candidate invariant.
Any top/current comparison is monotonic.
One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.

feedback.reason: Magnitude comparison decides a local collision, but retained asteroids are survivors in encounter order rather than unresolved ordered boundary candidates.

blocks.text: Only a right-moving top and left-moving current can collide; magnitude selects which object survives. The stack may contain arbitrary magnitudes and signs compatible with past collisions, not a declared increasing or decreasing key. A pop proves destruction in this collision, not dominance for future nearest-boundary answers. Therefore comparison and repeated pops are insufficient classification evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Top/current comparison also serves local collision rules; it does not imply a monotone frontier.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Indices, loops, or linear time still do not change survivor semantics into unresolved-candidate semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Survivors `[5,10]` happen to be sorted here, but another legal survivor sequence can break that order.

items.prompt: On leaving a scope, an interpreter repeatedly pops local declarations until it reaches that scope’s marker. Does the while-pop loop identify a monotonic stack?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Arity, cleanup, completion, and backtracking can pop multiple entries.
A while-pop loop uniquely identifies monotonic stacks.
One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.
If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.

feedback.reason: No. Scope exit removes entries until a structural marker, so repeated pops follow lifetime cleanup rather than a comparison invariant.

blocks.text: Each retained declaration belongs to an active scope. A close event repeatedly removes locals until the matching marker, regardless of their values. Similar repeated pops occur for operator arity and DFS backtracking. A monotonic pop instead removes a comparison-defined top suffix because those candidates are finalized or dominated. Loop shape alone cannot distinguish these proofs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: The loop stops at a structural marker, not when a monotone comparison relation is restored.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Repeated pops and linear runtime occur in both categories and therefore cannot classify them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Incidental payload order is irrelevant to scope ownership and cleanup.

items.prompt: Select all valid reasons that storing indices does not by itself identify a monotonic stack.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: A parser may retain token offsets for unmatched structural openers.
An explicit DFS stack may retain node indices as pending traversal work.
A monotonic stack may retain indices for distance or duplicate provenance, but its classification still comes from the ordered candidate invariant.
Indices are used only by monotonic-stack algorithms.
A value-only stack is necessarily ordinary and can never be monotonic.

feedback.reason: Indices are generic provenance: only retained-state meaning and an order-maintenance proof classify the algorithm.

blocks.text: A parser stores an opener offset to report a mismatch; DFS stores node IDs as pending work; a monotonic frontier stores indices to compute distance or preserve duplicate identity. These uses share provenance but not invariants. Conversely, a monotonic algorithm that needs only values can omit indices. Therefore all three accepted statements establish that payload shape is neither necessary nor sufficient.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Parser offsets and DFS node IDs are direct ordinary-stack counterexamples.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: A value-only frontier can still maintain a monotone key when the output does not require indices.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It shows ordinary structural state using indices for error provenance.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It shows ordinary pending-work state using indices as identity.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It states both the legitimate monotonic use and the separate semantic test.

items.prompt: Delimiter validation and next-greater processing both run in O(n) with constant-time stack operations. Does their shared complexity classify both as monotonic stacks?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.
If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.
Both ordinary and monotonic stack algorithms can be linear.
Linear time implies monotonic stack.

feedback.reason: No. Big-O describes work growth, while delimiter closure and ordered candidate finalization are different state semantics.

blocks.text: Delimiter validation visits each token and matches each opener once, yielding O(n). Next greater visits each item and uses at most one push and pop per candidate, also yielding O(n). The first stack represents unmatched structural ancestry; the second represents ordered unresolved candidates. Equal complexity is compatible with different correctness invariants, so it cannot determine the semantic category.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Linear time is a cost bound shared by many algorithms and says nothing about retained-entry meaning.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: None of the listed clues supplies the required order invariant and safe comparison-removal proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: A sorted snapshot does not explain either algorithm’s lifecycle and can be incidental.

items.prompt: Select all reasons that a push-once/pop-once amortized proof is insufficient to classify a stack as monotonic.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Monotonic classification additionally requires an ordered unresolved frontier and a safe relation-driven removal rule.
Any amortized O(n) proof automatically establishes a monotonic stack.
A nested while-loop is unique to monotonic-stack algorithms.
The proof bounds cost but does not state what retained entries mean.
An ordinary delimiter validator can also push and pop each opener at most once.

feedback.reason: Push-once/pop-once proves a transition bound; monotonic classification additionally requires ordered unresolved candidates and relation-driven safe removal.

blocks.text: The lifecycle proof counts transitions but does not say what an entry represents or why it is removed. A delimiter opener is pushed once and popped once when its closer arrives, yet no value order is maintained. A monotonic frontier adds a declared order and proves that the exact comparison finalizes or dominates each popped candidate. Nested while loops are likewise not unique: cleanup and collision algorithms use them too.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Delimiter validation has the same bounded lifecycle without being a monotonic-candidate algorithm.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Scope cleanup and collision resolution provide ordinary-stack while-loop counterexamples.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It separates a cost argument from a semantic invariant.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It supplies a concrete ordinary-stack algorithm with the same transition bound.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It names the positive order and removal evidence still required.

items.prompt: Unfamiliar code stores candidate records in a stack. What positive invariant must be proved before calling it a monotonic-stack algorithm?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: A declared key must remain monotone among unresolved candidates under every legal transition.
Any LIFO state qualifies without an order invariant.
One surface feature—such as a variable name, indices, comparisons, repeated pops, or linear time—is sufficient to classify the stack as monotonic.
If the retained values appear sorted at any one point in the trace, the algorithm is monotonic by definition.

feedback.reason: A declared comparison key must be monotone across all live unresolved candidates after every legal transition.

blocks.text: First identify each entry as an unresolved candidate for the requested output. Then state the key and direction—such as non-increasing values for strict next greater—and prove every push/pop preserves it. Finally connect removal to finalization or permanent irrelevance. LIFO alone covers many ordinary stacks; one sorted state is not inductive; names and complexity do not provide any of these proofs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: LIFO says which end is removed but provides no candidate key, order, or dominance proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The listed clues are compatible with ordinary stacks and do not establish the positive invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: One observed order can disappear on the next legal transition and is not a maintained invariant.

items.prompt: Select all parts of a complete positive test for classifying unfamiliar pseudocode as a monotonic-stack algorithm.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: The total running time is O(n), so the semantic category is determined.
Retained entries are unresolved candidates ordered by a declared key.
The current item removes candidates through an exact comparison relation.
The removal proof shows that each popped candidate is finalized or can never affect a future valid answer.
The code stores indices and contains a while-loop.

feedback.reason: The positive test requires ordered unresolved candidates, an exact comparison pop rule, and a proof that every removal is final or future-safe.

blocks.text: All three accepted facts are necessary. Candidate meaning and monotone key describe the live frontier; the exact current/top relation describes its maintenance; the removal proof connects that maintenance to the output. Indices and a while-loop also appear in parsers and DFS, while O(n) also describes delimiter validation. Those false clues are neither sufficient alone nor sufficient together without semantic evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Parsers and DFS can store indices and use while-loops without an ordered candidate frontier.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Linear time is a cost property shared by ordinary and monotonic stack algorithms.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It states the semantic role and the maintained order of live entries.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It identifies the transition that restores the frontier.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It proves the pop preserves the actual output contract.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Classify unfamiliar stack code from retained-state semantics, a maintained order invariant, the exact removal rule, and its correctness argument—not from names, indices, comparisons, loops, or asymptotic cost alone.
